claim: In wild-type Caenorhabditis elegans zygotes, symmetry breaking during anterior-posterior axis specification is guided by centrosomes, resulting in anterior-directed cortical flows and a single posterior PAR-2 domain.
source: In wild-type Caenorhabditis elegans zygotes, symmetry breaking during anterior-posterior axis specification is guided by centrosomes, resulting in anterior-directed cortical flows and a single posterior PAR-2 domain.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract summarizing established knowledge about wild-type C. elegans zygotes.

claim: C. elegans zygotes depleted of the Aurora A kinase AIR-1 usually establish two posterior PAR-2 domains, one at each pole.
source: We uncover that C. elegans zygotes depleted of the Aurora A kinase AIR-1 or lacking centrosomes entirely usually establish two posterior PAR-2 domains, one at each pole.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations presented in the manuscript, including time-lapse microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 1.

claim: C. elegans zygotes lacking centrosomes entirely usually establish two posterior PAR-2 domains, one at each pole.
source: We uncover that C. elegans zygotes depleted of the Aurora A kinase AIR-1 or lacking centrosomes entirely usually establish two posterior PAR-2 domains, one at each pole.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from centrosome ablation experiments and such-1 mutant sperm experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: AIR-1 prevents symmetry breaking early in the cell cycle.
source: We demonstrate that AIR-1 prevents symmetry breaking early in the cell cycle, whereas centrosomal AIR-1 instructs polarity initiation thereafter.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing cortical AIR-1 localization early in the cell cycle and experiments with membrane-targeted AIR-1 shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Centrosomal AIR-1 instructs polarity initiation after the early cell cycle.
source: We demonstrate that AIR-1 prevents symmetry breaking early in the cell cycle, whereas centrosomal AIR-1 instructs polarity initiation thereafter.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments showing that targeting AIR-1 to centrioles rescues polarity, as shown in Figure 7K-L.

claim: Bipolarity of air-1(RNAi) embryos occurs effectively in a cell-shape and curvature-dependent manner.
source: Using triangular microfabricated chambers, we establish that bipolarity of air-1(RNAi) embryos occurs effectively in a cell-shape and curvature-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments using triangular PDMS chambers shown in Figure 3.

claim: Local PAR-2-dependent weakening of the actin cortex, together with mutual inhibition of anterior and posterior PAR proteins, provides a mechanism for spontaneous symmetry breaking without centrosomes.
source: Furthermore, we develop an integrated physical description of symmetry breaking, wherein local PAR-2-dependent weakening of the actin cortex, together with mutual inhibition of anterior and posterior PAR proteins, provides a mechanism for spontaneous symmetry breaking without centrosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the theoretical modeling presented in Figure 4 and the Appendix, which integrates experimental observations into a physical framework.

claim: Approximately 76% of air-1(RNAi) embryos formed two PAR-2 domains, one at each pole, by the time of pronuclear meeting.
source: In stark contrast,~76% air-1(RNAi) embryos formed two PAR-2 domains, one at each pole (Figure 1B and C, Video 2, referred to as 'bipolar').
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Approximately 19% of air-1(RNAi) embryos established a single PAR-2 domain, usually on the side of the maternal pronucleus.
source: Another ~19% air-1(RNAi) embryos established a single PAR-2 domain, usually on the side of the maternal pronucleus (Figure 1C, referred to as 'anterior') or else on that of the male pronucleus (Figure 1C, referred to as 'posterior').
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Approximately 5% of air-1(RNAi) embryos harbored no plasma membrane PAR-2.
source: Moreover,~5% air-1(RNAi) embryos harbored no plasma membrane PAR-2 (Figure 1C, referred to as 'none').
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Progressive dilutions of air-1(RNAi) resulted in weaker spindle assembly defects and shifted the polarity phenotype away from harboring two poles.
source: We noted also that progressive dilutions of air-1(RNAi) resulted in weaker spindle assembly defects and shifted the polarity phenotype away from harboring two poles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Bipolarity is the most severe AIR-1 depletion phenotype obtained using RNAi, likely corresponding to a strong if not complete loss of function in the embryo.
source: Therefore, bipolarity is the most severe AIR-1 depletion phenotype obtained using RNAi, likely corresponding to a strong if not complete loss of function in the embryo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dilution experiments and the observation that null alleles of air-1 result in sterility.

claim: Null alleles of air-1 result in sterility, precluding their analysis in the embryo.
source: Note that null alleles of air-1 result in sterility (Furuta et al., 2002), precluding their analysis in the embryo.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Furuta et al., 2002.

claim: The fluorescence intensity of each of the two PAR-2 domains in air-1(RNAi) embryos was weaker than that of the single PAR-2 domain in control embryos.
source: We found that the fluorescence intensity of each of the two PAR-2 domains was weaker than that of the single PAR-2 domain in control embryos (Figure 1E,F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Each of the two PAR-2 domains in air-1(RNAi) embryos was smaller than the single PAR-2 domain in control embryos.
source: Likewise, each of the two PAR-2 domains was smaller (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The summed fluorescence intensities and sizes of both PAR-2 domains in air-1(RNAi) embryos did not differ significantly from that of the single PAR-2 domain in control embryos.
source: However, the summed fluorescence intensities and sizes of both PAR-2 domains did not differ significantly from that of the single PAR-2 domain in control embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Both PAR-6 and PKC-3 localized to the anterior pole in all control embryos.
source: Both PAR-6 and PKC-3 localized to the anterior pole in all control embryos but were restricted to the middle region in ~80% air-1(RNAi) embryos, as anticipated from the bipolar distribution of PAR-2 (Figure 1G–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1G-J.

claim: PAR-6 and PKC-3 were restricted to the middle region in approximately 80% of air-1(RNAi) embryos.
source: Both PAR-6 and PKC-3 localized to the anterior pole in all control embryos but were restricted to the middle region in ~80% air-1(RNAi) embryos, as anticipated from the bipolar distribution of PAR-2 (Figure 1G–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1H,J.

claim: MEX-5 was enriched in the anterior of control embryos in response to proper A-P polarity.
source: Furthermore, we found that the cytoplasmic polarity mediator protein MEX-5, which was enriched in the anterior of control embryos in response to proper A-P polarity (Schubert et al., 2000), was present primarily in the middle region of ~80% air-1(RNAi) embryos (Figure 1K,L).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1K and citation to Schubert et al., 2000.

claim: MEX-5 was present primarily in the middle region of approximately 80% of air-1(RNAi) embryos.
source: Furthermore, we found that the cytoplasmic polarity mediator protein MEX-5, which was enriched in the anterior of control embryos in response to proper A-P polarity (Schubert et al., 2000), was present primarily in the middle region of ~80% air-1(RNAi) embryos (Figure 1K,L).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Wild type GFP::AIR-1 rescued posterior PAR-2 polarity upon depletion of endogenous AIR-1 in approximately 63% of embryos.
source: We found that whereas wild type GFP::AIR-1 rescued posterior PAR-2 polarity upon depletion of endogenous AIR-1 in ~63% of embryos, the kinase inactive version did not, with all embryos being bipolar (Figure 1M,N).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1N.

claim: The kinase inactive version of GFP::AIR-1 did not rescue posterior PAR-2 polarity upon depletion of endogenous AIR-1, with all embryos being bipolar.
source: We found that whereas wild type GFP::AIR-1 rescued posterior PAR-2 polarity upon depletion of endogenous AIR-1 in ~63% of embryos, the kinase inactive version did not, with all embryos being bipolar (Figure 1M,N).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1N.

claim: AIR-1 kinase activity is required to ensure a unique symmetry breaking event in C. elegans zygotes.
source: Overall, we conclude that AIR-1 kinase activity is required to ensure a unique symmetry breaking event in C. elegans zygotes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments with kinase-inactive AIR-1 mutants.

claim: Control embryos exhibited anterior-directed movements of NMY-2 emanating from the centrosomes-bearing region, followed by the appearance of a posterior PAR-2 domain.
source: Examining cortical flows, we found that control embryos exhibited the expected anterior-directed movements of NMY-2 emanating from the centrosomes-bearing region, followed by the appearance of a posterior PAR-2 domain (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by kymograph data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Embryos depleted of AIR-1 exhibited cortical flows stemming from both poles and directed toward the embryo center, followed by PAR-2 domain establishment at both poles.
source: By contrast, embryos depleted of AIR-1 exhibited cortical flows stemming from both poles and directed toward the embryo center, followed by PAR-2 domain establishment at both poles (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by kymograph data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The average peak velocities of cortical flows were approximately 6.8 µm/min in control embryos.
source: Quantification of cortical flows using particle image velocimetry (PIV) of RFP::NMY-2 revealed that the average peak velocities were ~6.8 µm/min in control embryos, but ~3.1 µm/min for posterior- and ~2.9 µm/min for anterior-directed flows, respectively, in air-1(RNAi) embryos (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by PIV quantification data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The average peak velocities of cortical flows were approximately 3.1 µm/min for posterior-directed flows and approximately 2.9 µm/min for anterior-directed flows in air-1(RNAi) embryos.
source: Quantification of cortical flows using particle image velocimetry (PIV) of RFP::NMY-2 revealed that the average peak velocities were ~6.8 µm/min in control embryos, but ~3.1 µm/min for posterior- and ~2.9 µm/min for anterior-directed flows, respectively, in air-1(RNAi) embryos (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by PIV quantification data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The average peak velocities of the cortical flows in doubly depleted air-1(RNAi) rga-3(RNAi) embryos were close to those of control embryos.
source: We found that the average peak velocities of the cortical flows in doubly depleted air-1(RNAi) rga-3(RNAi) embryos were close to those of control embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by PIV quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The fraction of air-1(RNAi) rga-3(RNAi) embryos exhibiting a bipolar phenotype was not altered compared to air-1(RNAi) alone.
source: Despite this, the fraction of air-1(RNAi) rga-3(RNAi) embryos exhibiting a bipolar phenotype was not altered (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: While cortical flows are diminished upon AIR-1 depletion, this alone does not explain the bipolar phenotype.
source: Therefore, while cortical flows are diminished upon AIR-1 depletion, this alone does not explain the bipolar phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rga-3 co-depletion experiments.

claim: nmy-2(ne3409) embryos did not exhibit bipolarity and instead harbored a single posterior PAR-2 domain, which formed later and was smaller than in the control.
source: We found that nmy-2(ne3409) embryos did not exhibit bipolarity and instead harbored a single posterior PAR-2 domain, which formed later and was smaller than in the control (Figure 2G,H; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), in line with prior work (Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, and is consistent with prior work cited.

claim: Depletion of AIR-1 in nmy-2(ne3409) embryos almost completely abolished cortical flows.
source: Depletion of AIR-1 in nmy-2(ne3409) embryos almost completely abolished cortical flows (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), but small bipolar PAR-2 domains formed nevertheless in most embryos, although with a substantial delay (Figure 2G,H; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by PIV data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Small bipolar PAR-2 domains formed in most nmy-2(ne3409) air-1(RNAi) embryos, although with a substantial delay.
source: Depletion of AIR-1 in nmy-2(ne3409) embryos almost completely abolished cortical flows (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), but small bipolar PAR-2 domains formed nevertheless in most embryos, although with a substantial delay (Figure 2G,H; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Cortical acto-myosin flows present in air-1(RNAi) embryos are not essential for bipolarity, but contribute to the robustness and extent of the two PAR-2 domains.
source: Together, these findings indicate that cortical acto-myosin flows present in air-1(RNAi) embryos are not essential for bipolarity, but contribute to the robustness and extent of the two PAR-2 domains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the nmy-2(ne3409) experiments.

claim: Diminishing cortical flows by co-depletion of ECT-2 abolished loading of PAR-2 R163A and PAR-2 R183-5A mutants onto the plasma membrane.
source: As reported previously (Motegi et al., 2011), whereas all three transgenes rescued depletion of endogenous PAR-2 to almost 100%, diminishing cortical flows by co-depletion of ECT-2 abolished loading of the two PAR-2 mutants onto the plasma membrane (Figure 2I–K; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 2I-K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G-J, and is consistent with prior work cited.

claim: Co-depletion of AIR-1 with endogenous PAR-2 abolished loading of PAR-2 R163A and PAR-2 R183-5A mutants onto the plasma membrane.
source: Strikingly, we found the same to be true in these mutants when AIR-1 was co-depleted with endogenous PAR-2 (Figure 2I–K; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 2I-K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G-J.

claim: Cortical flows were normal when PAR-2 alone was depleted.
source: Moreover, whereas cortical flows were normal when PAR-2 alone was depleted (Munro et al., 2004) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K,M,N), we found that they were absent when AIR-1 was depleted concomitantly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1L,M,O), reflecting the feedback loop of membrane-bound PAR-2 onto cortical flows (Gross et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by kymograph data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K,M,N and citation to prior work.

claim: Cortical flows were absent when AIR-1 was depleted concomitantly with PAR-2.
source: Moreover, whereas cortical flows were normal when PAR-2 alone was depleted (Munro et al., 2004) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K,M,N), we found that they were absent when AIR-1 was depleted concomitantly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1L,M,O), reflecting the feedback loop of membrane-bound PAR-2 onto cortical flows (Gross et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by kymograph data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1L,M,O and citation to prior work.

claim: The bipolarity of air-1(RNAi) embryos relies on the PAR-2-dependent pathway.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that the bipolarity of air-1(RNAi) embryos relies on the PAR-2-dependent pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments with PAR-2 mutants deficient in microtubule binding.

claim: PAR-2 domains in air-1(RNAi) embryos formed within a corner of the triangle in triangular PDMS chambers, with one exception.
source: Remarkably, with one exception, PAR-2 domains in air-1(RNAi) embryos formed within a corner of the triangle (Figure 3C), usually in the corner where the embryo exhibited the highest degree of curvature before symmetry breaking (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: PAR-2 domains in air-1(RNAi) embryos usually formed in the corner where the embryo exhibited the highest degree of curvature before symmetry breaking.
source: Remarkably, with one exception, PAR-2 domains in air-1(RNAi) embryos formed within a corner of the triangle (Figure 3C), usually in the corner where the embryo exhibited the highest degree of curvature before symmetry breaking (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PAR-2 domains in air-1(RNAi) embryos formed independently of the position of centrosomes or polar bodies in triangular chambers.
source: Moreover, as shown in Figure 3E, PAR-2 domains in air-1(RNAi) embryos formed independently of the position of centrosomes or polar bodies, in contrast to control embryos, in which PAR-2 domain formation coincided simply with centrosome position.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Embryos depleted of AIR-1 recruit PAR-2 preferentially to curved regions.
source: Together, these experiments indicate that embryos depleted of AIR-1 recruit PAR-2 preferentially to curved regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the triangular chamber experiments.

claim: Immunofluorescence analysis did not reveal an accumulation of microtubules at the poles of air-1(RNAi) embryos.
source: However, immunofluorescence analysis did not reveal an accumulation of microtubules at the poles of air-1(RNAi) embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Removing microtubules from control embryos using nocodazole did not prevent posterior PAR-2 domain establishment.
source: As previously reported (Hayashi et al., 2012; Sonneville and Gönczy, 2004; Tsai and Ahringer, 2007), removing microtubules from control embryos did not prevent posterior PAR-2 domain establishment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G, and is consistent with prior work cited.

claim: Nocodazole-treated air-1(RNAi) embryos recruited PAR-2 to both poles.
source: Importantly, nocodazole-treated air-1(RNAi) embryos recruited PAR-2 to both poles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: Embryos lacking microtubules following RNAi-mediated depletion of the α-tubulin TBA-2 showed analogous results to nocodazole treatment.
source: We found an analogous result in embryos lacking microtubules following RNAi-mediated depletion of the α-tubulin TBA-2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The preference of PAR-2 for the polar regions of air-1(RNAi) embryos is not due to microtubule enrichment in those areas.
source: Overall, we conclude that the preference of PAR-2 for the polar regions of air-1(RNAi) embryos is not due to microtubule enrichment in those areas.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the microtubule depletion experiments.

claim: The physical description successfully captures the phenotypes of wild-type embryos, of embryos depleted of AIR-1, as well as of embryos placed in triangular chambers.
source: Regardless, the physical description we developed successfully captures the phenotypes of wild-type embryos, of embryos depleted of AIR-1, as well as of embryos placed in triangular chambers.
evidence: This claim is supported by the theoretical modeling results shown in Figure 4 and comparison with experimental data.

claim: Before symmetry breaking, GFP::AIR-1 localized in the vicinity of the cell cortex as well as in the cytoplasm, and was barely detectable at centrosomes.
source: Intriguingly, we found that, before symmetry breaking, GFP::AIR-1 localized in the vicinity of the cell cortex (hereafter referred to as 'cortical'), as well as in the cytoplasm, and was barely detectable at centrosomes (Figures 5A and 00:00).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: After symmetry breaking, the cortical and cytoplasmic pools of GFP::AIR-1 decreased, which was paralleled by an increase of GFP::AIR-1 at maturing centrosomes.
source: Thereafter, the cortical and cytoplasmic pools decreased, which was paralleled by an increase of GFP::AIR-1 at maturing centrosomes (Figures 5A and 08:00-15:00).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Wild-type embryos stained for endogenous AIR-1 showed the same spatio-temporal distribution as GFP::AIR-1.
source: We found the same spatio-temporal distribution in wild-type embryos stained for endogenous AIR-1 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: GFP::AIR-1 co-localized with mCherry::TBA-2.
source: Since the distribution of cortical AIR-1 is reminiscent of that of microtubules (O'Rourke et al., 2010), we assessed whether GFP::AIR-1 co-localized with mCherry::TBA-2, and found this to be the case indeed (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5C and citation to prior work.

claim: Endogenous AIR-1 co-localized with cortical microtubules before symmetry breaking in wild-type embryos.
source: Likewise, endogenous AIR-1 co-localized with cortical microtubules before symmetry breaking in wild-type embryos (Figure 5H; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cortical AIR-1 was lost upon nocodazole-mediated depletion of microtubules.
source: Importantly, we found that cortical AIR-1 was lost upon nocodazole-mediated depletion of microtubules (Figure 5E,I), whereas the centrosomal pool of AIR-1 was unaffected (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5E,I.

claim: The centrosomal pool of AIR-1 was unaffected by nocodazole-mediated depletion of microtubules.
source: Importantly, we found that cortical AIR-1 was lost upon nocodazole-mediated depletion of microtubules (Figure 5E,I), whereas the centrosomal pool of AIR-1 was unaffected (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Depletion of AIR-1 did not alter the localization of cortical microtubules, but led to a slight increase in the corresponding signal intensity.
source: In contrast, depletion of AIR-1 did not alter the localization of cortical microtubules, but led to a slight increase in the corresponding signal intensity (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Cortical AIR-1 does not modulate polarity establishment.
source: Overall, given that the absence of microtubules does not prevent A-P polarity (Cowan and Hyman, 2004; Sonneville and Gönczy, 2004; Tsai and Ahringer, 2007), these experiments lead us to propose that cortical AIR-1 does not modulate polarity establishment and that AIR-1 functions instead elsewhere, presumably in the cytoplasm, to prevent aberrant symmetry breaking early in the cell cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the microtubule depletion experiments and prior work cited.

claim: AIR-1 functions in the cytoplasm to prevent aberrant symmetry breaking early in the cell cycle.
source: Overall, given that the absence of microtubules does not prevent A-P polarity (Cowan and Hyman, 2004; Sonneville and Gönczy, 2004; Tsai and Ahringer, 2007), these experiments lead us to propose that cortical AIR-1 does not modulate polarity establishment and that AIR-1 functions instead elsewhere, presumably in the cytoplasm, to prevent aberrant symmetry breaking early in the cell cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the microtubule depletion experiments and prior work cited.

claim: Mutant alleles of spd-2 and spd-5 exhibit the same bipolar phenotype as air-1(RNAi) embryos.
source: Importantly, we observed the same bipolar phenotype in mutant alleles of spd-2 and spd-5 (Figure 7A,B), as indicated previously (Hamill et al., 2002; O'Connell et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7A,B, and is consistent with prior work cited.

claim: Depleting TBG-1 does not impact polarity.
source: By contrast, we found that depleting TBG-1, which is recruited to centrosomes in an AIR-1-dependent manner and is required for MTOC activity, does not impact polarity (Figure 7A,B) (Hannak et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7A,B, and is consistent with prior work cited.

claim: Embryos derived from such-1(t1668) mutant sperm that lack centrioles usually establish a bipolar or an anterior PAR-2 domain.
source: Strikingly, we found that such embryos usually establish a bipolar or an anterior PAR-2 domain (Figure 7D,E), indicating that centrosomes are dispensable for PAR-2 plasma membrane loading.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: Centrosomes are dispensable for PAR-2 plasma membrane loading.
source: Strikingly, we found that such embryos usually establish a bipolar or an anterior PAR-2 domain (Figure 7D,E), indicating that centrosomes are dispensable for PAR-2 plasma membrane loading.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the such-1 mutant sperm experiments.

claim: Six out of nine embryos established bipolar GFP::PAR-2 domains upon centrosome ablation, with the remaining three developing an anterior PAR-2 domain.
source: Importantly, we found that six out of nine embryos established bipolar GFP::PAR-2 domains upon centrosome ablation, with the remaining three developing an anterior PAR-2 domain (Figure 7F–H, Video 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7F-H and Video 8.

claim: C. elegans embryos undergo spontaneous symmetry breaking in an unregulated manner in the absence of centrioles and centrosomes.
source: Together, these experiments lead to the unequivocal conclusion that C. elegans embryos undergo spontaneous symmetry breaking in an unregulated manner in the absence of centrioles and centrosomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the centrosome ablation and such-1 mutant experiments.

claim: Most air-1(RNAi) embryos were bipolar even in cases where both male and female pronuclei were on the same side of the embryo.
source: Importantly, we found that most air-1(RNAi) embryos were bipolar even in those cases where both male and female pronuclei were on the same side of the embryo (Figure 7I,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7I,J.

claim: Localizing GBP::mCherry::AIR-1 to centrioles by crossing GFP::SAS-7 in this strain rescued posterior polarity of mCherry::PAR-2 in the majority of embryos.
source: Strikingly, we found that localizing GBP::mCherry::AIR-1 to centrioles by crossing GFP::SAS-7 in this strain rescued posterior polarity of mCherry::PAR-2 in the majority of embryos (Figure 7K,L), although the PAR-2 domain was smaller compared to the control condition (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7K,L.

claim: AIR-1 localized on centrioles is sufficient to impart substantial posterior polarity.
source: We conclude that AIR-1 localized on centrioles is sufficient to impart substantial posterior polarity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GBP::mCherry::AIR-1 targeting experiments.

claim: AIR-1 exerts a dual role in symmetry breaking, acting early in the cell cycle, possibly in the cytoplasm, to prevent spontaneous polarization and at centrosomes thereafter to define the future posterior of the animal.
source: We propose that AIR-1 exerts a dual role in this process, acting early in the cell cycle, possibly in the cytoplasm, to prevent spontaneous polarization and at centrosomes thereafter to define the future posterior of the animal.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the absence of either AIR-1 or of centrosomes, embryos become bipolar, with PAR-2 domains at both poles.
source: In the absence of either AIR-1 or of centrosomes, embryos become bipolar, with PAR-2 domains at both poles.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main experimental findings.

claim: The C. elegans zygote possesses the ability to spontaneously form polarity domains in a centrosome-independent manner at the onset of development.
source: Overall, our work reveals that the C. elegans zygote possesses the ability to spontaneously form polarity domains in a centrosome-independent manner at the onset of development.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main conclusion of the work.

claim: SPD-2 and SPD-5 are needed for cortical AIR-1 distribution, in addition to their known requirement for centrosomal AIR-1 recruitment.
source: We found also that SPD-2 and SPD-5 are needed for cortical AIR-1 distribution, in addition to their known requirement for centrosomal AIR-1 recruitment.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5F,G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Targeting excess AIR-1 to the vicinity of the plasma membrane is generally sufficient to prevent PAR-2 recruitment throughout the embryo, in a manner independent of SPD-2 and SPD-5.
source: We found in addition that targeting excess AIR-1 to the vicinity of the plasma membrane is generally sufficient to prevent PAR-2 recruitment throughout the embryo, in a manner independent of SPD-2 and SPD-5.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments shown in Figure 6B,C using GBP::mCherry::AIR-1 targeted to the membrane via GFP::PH.

claim: Endogenous cortical or cytoplasmic AIR-1 can limit the expansion of an anterior PAR-2 domain upon delayed meiotic cell cycle progression.
source: Furthermore, we found that endogenous cortical or cytoplasmic AIR-1 can limit the expansion of an anterior PAR-2 domain upon delayed meiotic cell cycle progression, and thus could be of importance under environmental stress conditions that cause such delays (Davis-Roca et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments with mat-1(ax161) mutants shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Targeting GBP::mCh::AIR-1 to centrioles in embryos depleted of SPD-2 is sufficient to recruit PAR-2 to the neighboring plasma membrane.
source: We found that targeting GBP::mCh::AIR-1 to centrioles in embryos depleted of SPD-2, and thereby of microtubule nucleation activity, is sufficient to recruit PAR-2 to the neighboring plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments shown in Figure 7K,L.

claim: The position of centrosomes within the embryo determines the location of symmetry breaking and of PAR-2 recruitment to the plasma membrane in wild-type C. elegans zygotes.
source: Indeed, the position of centrosomes within the embryo determines the location of symmetry breaking and of PAR-2 recruitment to the plasma membrane (Bienkowska and Cowan, 2012; Cowan and Hyman, 2004; Cuenca et al., 2003; Goldstein and Hird, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The mechanism that governs spontaneous polarization of the zygote in the absence of AIR-1 or of centrosomes is largely independent of cortical flows.
source: The mechanism that governs spontaneous polarization of the zygote in the absence of AIR-1 or of centrosomes is largely independent of cortical flows.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the nmy-2(ne3409) experiments.

claim: Two PAR-2 domains can form in nmy-2(ne3409) air-1(RNAi) embryos, where cortical flows are essentially absent or below the detection limit.
source: Indeed, two PAR-2 domains can form in nmy-2(ne3409) air-1(RNAi) embryos, where cortical flows are essentially absent or below the detection limit.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and PIV data shown in Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PAR-2 domains in nmy-2(ne3409) air-1(RNAi) embryos are significantly smaller and develop later than in air-1(RNAi) embryos.
source: However, PAR-2 domains in such embryos are significantly smaller and develop later than in air-1(RNAi) embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The mechanism leading to spontaneous polarization in the absence of AIR-1 or of centrosomes functions independently of microtubules.
source: Our findings also establish that the mechanism leading to spontaneous polarization in the absence of AIR-1 or of centrosomes functions independently of microtubules.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the nocodazole and tba-2(RNAi) experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-H.

claim: Polarized membrane domains can be initiated largely independently of cortical flows through the instability of the PAR system, but cortical flows help sharpen and accelerate polarization of the embryo.
source: In conclusion, our findings indicate that polarized membrane domains can be initiated largely independently of cortical flows through the instability of the PAR system, but that cortical flows help sharpen and accelerate polarization of the embryo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the various experiments examining the role of cortical flows.

claim: PAR-2 indirectly reduces cortical contractility via antagonism with PAR-6.
source: Instead, we assumed that PAR-2 indirectly reduces cortical contractility via antagonism with PAR-6 (Gross et al., 2019).
evidence: This assumption in the theoretical model is based on prior work cited.

claim: Dissociation rates of cortical NMY-2 are regulated by PAR proteins, with lower dissociation rates occurring in the PAR-6-containing domain than in the PAR-2-containing domain.
source: It has been shown that dissociation rates of cortical NMY-2 are regulated by PAR proteins, with lower dissociation rates occurring in the PAR-6-containing domain than in the PAR-2-containing domain (Gross et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The physical description successfully captures the phenotypes of wild-type embryos, of embryos depleted of AIR-1, as well as of embryos placed in triangular chambers.
source: Regardless, the physical description we developed successfully captures the phenotypes of wild-type embryos, of embryos depleted of AIR-1, as well as of embryos placed in triangular chambers.
evidence: This claim is supported by the theoretical modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The PAR-2 domain relaxes to the nearby pole even if the initial active stress reduction occurred laterally.
source: Interestingly, this dynamical system also predicted that the PAR-2 domain relaxes to the nearby pole even if the initial active stress reduction occurred laterally (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Lateral sperm entry in control embryos results in PAR-2 domain relaxation to the pole.
source: This has been observed experimentally following lateral sperm entry in control embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D) (Goldstein and Hird, 1996) or upon displacement of the PAR-2 domain from the pole using light-induced cytoplasmic streaming (Mittasch et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D and citations to prior work.

claim: Relaxation of the PAR-2 domain was observed in air-1(RNAi) embryos, although in a less robust manner than in the wild type, likely due to impaired cortical flows.
source: This relaxation of the PAR-2 domain was also observed in air-1(RNAi) embryos, although in a less robust manner than in the wild type, likely due to impaired cortical flows (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: SPD-2 and SPD-5 are required for cortical AIR-1 distribution and for limiting the intensity of the cortical microtubule network signal.
source: Interestingly, we found that SPD-2 or SPD-5, which are both required to recruit AIR-1 to centrosomes (Hamill et al., 2002; Kemp et al., 2004), are also needed for the presence of AIR-1 at the cell cortex, as well as for limiting the intensity of the cortical microtubule network signal (Figure 5F,G; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5F,G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, and citations to prior work.

claim: Microtubules, SPD-2, SPD-5 and AIR-1 kinase activity are needed for the presence of AIR-1 at the cell cortex early in the cell cycle.
source: Overall, we conclude that microtubules, SPD-2, SPD-5 and AIR-1 kinase activity are needed for the presence of AIR-1 at the cell cortex early in the cell cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the various experiments examining cortical AIR-1 localization.

claim: Wild-type GFP::AIR-1 was both cortical and centrosomal.
source: Although wild-type GFP::AIR-1 was both cortical and centrosomal, as anticipated, the kinase inactive version did not localize to the cortex and barely to the centrosomes (Figure 5J,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5J,K.

claim: The kinase inactive version of GFP::AIR-1 did not localize to the cortex and barely to the centrosomes.
source: Although wild-type GFP::AIR-1 was both cortical and centrosomal, as anticipated, the kinase inactive version did not localize to the cortex and barely to the centrosomes (Figure 5J,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5J,K.

claim: The GBP::mCherry::AIR-1 fusion protein rescued depletion of endogenous AIR-1 in approximately 67% of embryos.
source: The GBP::mCherry::AIR-1 fusion protein rescued depletion of endogenous AIR-1 in ~67% of embryos, demonstrating that it possesses substantial activity (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Co-depleting endogenous AIR-1 and SPD-2 in the presence of GBP::mCherry::AIR-1 resulted primarily in bipolar embryos as scored by mCherry::PAR-2.
source: As anticipated, co-depleting endogenous AIR-1 and SPD-2 in the presence of GBP::mCherry::AIR-1 resulted primarily in bipolar embryos as scored by mCherry::PAR-2 (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Recruiting GBP::mCherry::AIR-1 to the vicinity of the plasma membrane prevented PAR-2 domain formation in approximately 72% of embryos.
source: Importantly, we found that recruiting GBP::mCherry::AIR-1 to the vicinity of the plasma membrane prevented PAR-2 domain formation in ~72% of embryos, demonstrating that an excess of cortical AIR-1 can prevent symmetry breaking (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: An excess of cortical AIR-1 can prevent symmetry breaking.
source: Importantly, we found that recruiting GBP::mCherry::AIR-1 to the vicinity of the plasma membrane prevented PAR-2 domain formation in ~72% of embryos, demonstrating that an excess of cortical AIR-1 can prevent symmetry breaking (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the membrane-targeted AIR-1 experiments.

claim: Approximately 19% of mat-1(ax161) embryos developed a PAR-2 domain on the anterior side when shifted to 24°C for 2 hr.
source: When shifted to 24°C for 2 hr,~19% of mat-1(ax161) embryos developed a PAR-2 domain on the anterior side (Figure 6D,E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), a percentage that climbed to ~67% after 12 hr at 24°C (6D,E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Approximately 67% of mat-1(ax161) embryos developed a PAR-2 domain on the anterior side when shifted to 24°C for 12 hr.
source: When shifted to 24°C for 2 hr,~19% of mat-1(ax161) embryos developed a PAR-2 domain on the anterior side (Figure 6D,E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), a percentage that climbed to ~67% after 12 hr at 24°C (6D,E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Approximately 39% of mat-1(ax161) air-1(RNAi) embryos developed an anterior PAR-2 domain after 2 hr at 24°C.
source: Strikingly, we found that ~39% mat-1(ax161) air-1(RNAi) embryos developed an anterior PAR-2 domain after 2 hr, and ~79% after 12 hr (Figure 6D,E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Approximately 79% of mat-1(ax161) air-1(RNAi) embryos developed an anterior PAR-2 domain after 12 hr at 24°C.
source: Strikingly, we found that ~39% mat-1(ax161) air-1(RNAi) embryos developed an anterior PAR-2 domain after 2 hr, and ~79% after 12 hr (Figure 6D,E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PAR-2 domains were more robust in mat-1(ax161) air-1(RNAi) embryos compared to the mat-1(ax161) mutant alone.
source: Moreover, PAR-2 domains were more robust in mat-1(ax161) air-1(RNAi) embryos compared to the mat-1(ax161) mutant alone (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Endogenous levels of cortical or cytoplasmic AIR-1 can negatively regulate polarity establishment upon compromised meiotic progression.
source: Taken together, these findings establish that endogenous levels of cortical or cytoplasmic AIR-1 can also negatively regulate polarity establishment upon compromised meiotic progression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mat-1(ax161) experiments.

claim: In control embryos, approximately 50% of cases had centrioles along one side of the triangle and in the remaining approximately 50% in one of the corners in triangular PDMS chambers.
source: Despite being deformed, control embryos established a single PAR-2 domain in the vicinity of centrioles, which in ~50% of cases were along one side of the triangle and in the remaining ~50% in one of the corners (Figure 3A,B, Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A,B and Video 3.

claim: Approximately 20% of air-1(RNAi) embryos formed two PAR-2 domains in triangular PDMS chambers, with the remaining approximately 80% forming one domain.
source: Approximately 20% of air-1(RNAi) embryos formed two PAR-2 domains, with the remaining ~80% forming one domain (Figure 3A,B, Videos 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All control embryos established a single PAR-2 domain on the side of the centrosomes and the male pronucleus by the time of pronuclear meeting.
source: As anticipated, by the time of pronuclear meeting, all control embryos established a single PAR-2 domain on the side of the centrosomes and the male pronucleus (Figure 1A and C, Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 1A,C and Video 1.

claim: The zygote of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans is a powerful model system for dissecting the mechanisms that govern symmetry breaking and anterior-posterior (A-P) axis specification.
source: The zygote of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans is a powerful model system for dissecting the mechanisms that govern symmetry breaking and anterior-posterior (A-P) axis specification (reviewed in Rose and Gonczy, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Shortly after fertilization, the C. elegans zygote undergoes the two female meiotic divisions, leading to extrusion of the polar bodies, usually at the future anterior pole.
source: Shortly after fertilization, the zygote undergoes the two female meiotic divisions, leading to extrusion of the polar bodies, usually at the future anterior pole.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: The cell cortex is isotropic at the early stage of C. elegans zygote development, as evidenced by uniform acto-myosin contractions driven by the small GTPase RHO-1.
source: The cell cortex is isotropic at this early stage, as evidenced by uniform acto-myosin contractions driven by the small GTPase RHO-1.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: The RHO-1 guanine-nucleotide-exchange factor (GEF) ECT-2 is cleared from the cortex in the vicinity of the sperm-contributed centrioles, leading to local RHO-1 inactivation and cortical weakening.
source: Thereafter, the RHO-1 guanine-nucleotide-exchange factor (GEF) ECT-2 is cleared from the cortex in the vicinity of the sperm-contributed centrioles, which are usually located on the opposite side from the polar bodies, leading to local RHO-1 inactivation and cortical weakening (Motegi and Sugimoto, 2006; Zonies et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The posterior polarity proteins PAR-2 and PAR-1 become enriched at the location near the sperm-contributed centrioles.
source: Concomitantly, the posterior polarity proteins PAR-2 and PAR-1 become enriched at that location, whereas flows of the acto-myosin cortex transport the anterior PAR complex (PAR-3/PAR-6/PKC-3) away from this region, resulting in polarization along the A-P embryonic axis.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about C. elegans polarity establishment.

claim: Flows of the acto-myosin cortex transport the anterior PAR complex (PAR-3/PAR-6/PKC-3) away from the region near the sperm-contributed centrioles, resulting in polarization along the A-P embryonic axis.
source: Concomitantly, the posterior polarity proteins PAR-2 and PAR-1 become enriched at that location, whereas flows of the acto-myosin cortex transport the anterior PAR complex (PAR-3/PAR-6/PKC-3) away from this region, resulting in polarization along the A-P embryonic axis.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about C. elegans polarity establishment.

claim: Polarization arises from coupling advective cortical flows with a PAR reaction-diffusion system, whereby anterior PAR complex components antagonize plasma membrane binding of posterior PAR proteins.
source: Theoretical analysis based on measured rate constants indicates that polarization arises from coupling advective cortical flows with a PAR reaction-diffusion system, whereby anterior PAR complex components antagonize plasma membrane binding of posterior PAR proteins (Goehring et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: In the absence of cortical flows, a partially redundant pathway can polarize the embryo along the A-P axis.
source: In the absence of cortical flows, a partially redundant pathway can polarize the embryo along the A-P axis (Motegi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The partially redundant pathway relies on PAR-2 itself, through an ability to bind phosphoinositides and microtubules nucleated by the two centrosomes located at the future embryo posterior.
source: The available evidence indicates that this pathway relies on PAR-2 itself, through an ability to bind phosophinositides and microtubules nucleated by the two centrosomes located at the future embryo posterior.
evidence: This is a statement summarizing prior work on the PAR-2-dependent pathway.

claim: The PAR-2-dependent pathway serves to shield PAR-2 from the antagonizing effects of the anterior complex component PKC-3.
source: This serves to shield PAR-2 from the antagonizing effects of the anterior complex component PKC-3.
evidence: This is a statement summarizing prior work on the PAR-2-dependent pathway.

claim: The PAR-2-dependent pathway entails a positive feedback loop of membrane-bound PAR proteins onto dissociation rates of the non-muscle myosin NMY-2, which can induce weak cortical flows without a posterior trigger such as that provided by the centrosomes.
source: This second pathway also entails a positive feedback loop of membrane-bound PAR proteins onto dissociation rates of the non-muscle myosin NMY-2, which can induce weak cortical flows without a posterior trigger such as that provided by the centrosomes (Gross et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Zygotes arrested for several hours in metaphase of the first meiotic division, owing to a mutation in the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) component MAT-1, recruit PAR-2 to the plasma membrane in the vicinity of the meiotic spindle.
source: Furthermore, zygotes arrested for several hours in metaphase of the first meiotic division, owing to a mutation in the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) component MAT-1, recruit PAR-2 to the plasma membrane in the vicinity of the meiotic spindle, presumably due to the persistence of astral microtubules (Wallenfang and Seydoux, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: At the least under some circumstances other areas of the cell cortex are competent to recruit PAR-2.
source: This indicates that at the least under some circumstances other areas of the cell cortex are competent to recruit PAR-2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mat-1 mutant observations.

claim: In the wild type, both local RHO-1 inactivation and PAR-2-dependent pathways are thought to rely on centrosomes.
source: In the wild type, both local RHO-1 inactivation and PAR-2-dependent pathways are thought to rely on centrosomes.
evidence: This is a statement of the prevailing view prior to this work.

claim: Centrosomes were thought to be necessary for A-P polarity based on experiments in which centrosomes were ablated prior to polarity establishment using a laser microbeam, which resulted in the absence of PAR-2 from the entire cell cortex.
source: This inference is based primarily on experiments in which centrosomes were ablated prior to polarity establishment using a laser microbeam, which resulted in the absence of PAR-2 from the entire cell cortex (Cowan and Hyman, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Centrosomes assemble in the C. elegans zygote around the pair of centrioles contributed by the sperm, in a manner that depends on the coiled-proteins SPD-2 and SPD-5.
source: Centrosomes assemble in the C. elegans zygote around the pair of centrioles contributed by the sperm, in a manner that depends on the coiled-proteins SPD-2 and SPD-5 (Hamill et al., 2002; Kemp et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Centrosome maturation occurs during the first cell cycle, and entails notably recruitment to the pericentriolar material (PCM) of the Aurora A kinase AIR-1 and then of γ-tubulin (TBG-1).
source: Centrosome maturation occurs thereafter during the first cell cycle, and entails notably recruitment to the pericentriolar material (PCM) of the Aurora A kinase AIR-1 and then of γ-tubulin (TBG-1) (Toya et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Both AIR-1 and TBG-1 are required for full microtubule organizing center (MTOC) activity of centrosomes, and thus for bipolar spindle assembly and chromosome segregation.
source: Both AIR-1 and TBG-1 are required for full microtubule organizing center (MTOC) activity of centrosomes, and thus for bipolar spindle assembly and chromosome segregation (Hannak et al., 2001; Schumacher et al., 1998; Toya et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The mechanisms through which centrosomes instruct symmetry breaking in C. elegans remain unclear.
source: Despite the postulated essential role of centrosomes in A-P polarity and the knowledge about components critical for assembling them, the mechanisms through which centrosomes instruct symmetry breaking in C. elegans remain unclear.
evidence: This is a statement of the knowledge gap that this work addresses.

claim: Whether distinct polarization mechanisms might exist in zygotes deprived of centrosomes from the very onset of development has not been investigated.
source: Moreover, whether distinct polarization mechanisms might exist in zygotes deprived of centrosomes from the very onset of development has not been investigated.
evidence: This is a statement of the knowledge gap that this work addresses.
